reasoning: The study generated new research data: original PET imaging (11C-PBR28, 18F-flortaucipir), MRI, neuropsychological, and neuropathology data collected from 8 svPPA patients and control cohorts (D1 - data generated). For software, the paper uses established research tools (PMOD, SPM12, FreeSurfer, MATLAB curve-fitting toolbox) to process and analyze the data, but does not claim to have created or significantly extended any of these software packages - they are used as analysis utilities rather than being a contribution of the paper (S2 - software used).

The paper reports a new observational campaign: the authors obtained spectra and measured 3147 spectroscopic host-galaxy redshifts for Pan-STARRS SN candidates using multiple telescopes (AAT, APO, MMT, SDSS, WIYN), clearly generating new research data. They also developed their own implementation of the BEAMS Bayesian estimation method for this study, which they made available on GitHub (https://github.com/djones1040/BEAMS) with example input files — this is research software they created (beyond simply using existing tools like SNANA, SALT2, emcee, or CosmoMC, which are used but not the paper's contribution). Since software/data generation implies use, and generated artifacts take precedence over merely-used ones, this is S1D1.

The paper uses standard statistical software (R, mgcv, jtrans packages) only as analysis tools, not as a research software contribution of its own, so no research software was generated or claimed as a contribution (S3). The study generated new research data through an original field experiment (artificial tick infestation, blood/haematology assays, PBMC proliferation assays, ELISA, and PTPRC genotyping of 34 cattle), which constitutes data generation (D1).

This is a conceptual/theoretical paper that reviews literature on bureaucracy and the Balanced Scorecard, building an analytical framework (a "conceptual matrix" mapping nine bureaucracy concepts to BSC features) purely through literature review and argumentation. The authors explicitly state "This paper does not offer empirical support for the arguments made," confirming no research data was collected, generated, or analyzed, and no research software was created or used.

This is a review article (Energies, 2023) that surveys and synthesizes existing literature on energy storage for renewable-energy-powered water desalination systems. The authors do not report conducting their own experiments, simulations, or developing/using any research software, nor do they generate or use any research dataset—they only summarize findings and figures from cited third-party studies. The Data Availability Statement explicitly states "Not applicable." Hence no software (S3) and no research data (D3) are claimed.

The paper uses existing machine learning tools (Weka, JADBio) and an existing SANN method from prior work rather than developing new software, so it falls under Software Used (S2). It also collects new data for the proposed Autism Screening Tool for Adults (ASTA) questionnaires—administering novel 15- and 20-question surveys to 30 and 18 patients respectively and analyzing the resulting responses—constituting newly generated research data, in addition to using an existing 192-patient diagnostic dataset. Since new data was generated, the paper is classified as Data Generated (D1).

The paper develops a novel hierarchical energy management system (HLEM with MILP optimization, ANFIS forecasting, and an RTPC with adaptive autoregression) and implements this as custom code/scripts in MATLAB and LabVIEW, which also controls a real experimental microgrid via CAN bus — this is bespoke research software created for the study (S1), not merely use of generic tools (MATLAB/LabVIEW themselves are used as platforms, but the algorithms/control logic are the authors' own contribution). While some input data (CREST load model profiles, SODA weather data, PVOutput.org PV generation data) were existing/used data, the paper also generates new data through simulation results (forecasted/seasonal profiles, cost/SOC results) and through the laboratory experimental verification (real-time measurements of load, PV generation, SOC, and BESS settings), which constitutes newly generated research data (D1). Since generated artifacts take precedence over used ones, the paper is classified as S1D1.

The paper generated new research data: original field recordings and 360° video/audio collected at Peace Gardens, four designed experimental soundscape samples, and survey/questionnaire data from 120 participants, which were deposited on Mendeley Data (D1). No research software was created; the authors only used generic utility tools (SPSS, Matlab, Adobe Audition) for statistical analysis, clustering, and audio editing, which are not claimed as research contributions in their own right (S3).

The paper generated original research data by collecting behavioral observations of two Palawan binturong via CCTV cameras over multiple days, creating a novel dataset of activity patterns and behavior categories (D1: data generated). For analysis, they used R, which is generic statistical software (akin to STATA) not claimed as a research software contribution, and data entry was done via Microsoft Excel (also generic/non-research software). There is no claim of creating or significantly extending research software (S3: no research software)."

The paper only mentions use of SAS software for statistical analysis, which is generic statistical software and not research software, and no other software is claimed to be created or used as a research contribution, so S3. The paper reports a post-hoc analysis of the SSaSS cluster randomised trial, which collected new clinical/outcome data (cancer events, hospitalisation and mortality records) from 20,996 participants through original trial fieldwork—this constitutes newly generated research data, so D1.

The study used established existing research software tools (SPM12/DCM10, FreeSurfer, FSL, 3D Slicer, ICN_Atlas, SEEGA) for analysis without creating or extending any new software, qualifying as S2. The researchers prospectively collected new EEG-fMRI, structural MRI, and clinical/SEEG data from a cohort of 10 epilepsy patients specifically for this study, constituting newly generated research data (D1).

This is a narrative review discussing and synthesizing findings from existing GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on the genetic link between type 2 diabetes and cancer. The authors do not create or use any research software as a contribution (no tools, code, or pipelines are described), so S3 applies. They draw on and discuss findings/statistics derived from existing published genetic studies/datasets without generating new research data themselves, fitting D2 (data used).

The paper develops a conceptual/agile management model (not software) and validates it with two real-world case studies. The authors collected new empirical data through Gemba walks, brainstorming sessions, interviews, and direct observation of production shop floors (e.g., Tables 2–5: production lead times, uptime, ergonomics issues, environmental conditions), which constitutes research data generated from fieldwork. No research software is created or used—mentions like "design software to decide optimum path planning" are only proposed future actions, not actual software developed or used in the study. The Data Availability Statement ("data... available on request") further confirms original data was generated.

The paper analyzes the Russian Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS), an existing panel dataset created by other institutions (G-7 funders, USAID, World Bank, Carolina Population Center, HSE) that the authors use but did not create or significantly restructure, so this is Data Used (D2). The paper does not claim to develop or extend any research software; it applies standard econometric techniques (fixed-effects regressions, an existing ordered logit "blowup and cluster" estimator from prior literature) without naming or claiming contribution of any specific software tool, so this falls under No Research Software (S3).

This is a pure theoretical linear algebra paper presenting definitions, theorems, and proofs about matrix symmetry decompositions, illustrated with a worked numerical example (the Wilson matrix). There is no claim of creating or using research software (any numerical computation, e.g. SVD values, is incidental illustration, not a software contribution), and the paper's own Data Availability statement confirms "No data was used for the research described in the article." Hence no software and no data.

The paper uses an existing numerical model/code for rotating convection (described in Willis et al. 2007, "available on request"), with no claim of creating or significantly extending the software itself—this is S2 (software used). The paper runs a large new suite of numerical simulations (68+ simulations plus 6 additional with new hemispheric forcing) producing new simulation output data (temperature/velocity fields), which constitutes newly generated research data—this is D1. Plotting tools (VisIt, Matplotlib, seaborn) are generic/utility and don't count as research software contributions.

The paper exclusively uses existing third-party tools (Napu pipeline, Sniffles2, EMBOSS/Transeq, FASTA, BLAST, RepeatMasker, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, RIdeogram, Plotrix) without creating or significantly extending any software of its own, so it is S2 (software used). The sequencing data analyzed were pre-existing publicly available samples from the NABEC cohort (dbGaP accession), not newly generated by the authors; they derived novel findings/statistics from this existing dataset, which fits D2 (data used) rather than D1.

The paper uses existing surveillance/case data (WHO laboratory-confirmed MERS-CoV cases, traveler volume and trip-length statistics, population data) to derive estimates via a mathematical formula; these are statistics derived from existing data sources, which falls under D2 (Research Data Used), not D1, since no new dataset was generated or substantially restructured. No research software is claimed to have been created or used—only a calculation formula and standard statistical tests (Fisher exact test, profile-likelihood CIs) are applied, which do not constitute research software, so this is S3.

The study generated new research data: field-collected shark/copepod specimens and newly produced histological sections/images analyzed for this paper. No research software is mentioned or used (only generic lab equipment like an autostainer), so it is S3; the novel histopathological data generated classifies it as D1.

The paper generates substantial new research data: 44 newly isolated and sequenced flavobacterial phage genomes, host bacterial genomes/16S rRNA sequences, and North Sea metagenomic/viral abundance data collected during spring blooms (D1). For software, the authors exclusively use existing third-party tools for assembly, clustering, phylogenetics, and annotation (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, VIRIDIC, MUSCLE, IQ-Trees, FigTree, CRISPRCasFinder, WIsH, MiGA, ARB, RAxML, Geneious) and reference a bioinformatics annotation pipeline "described elsewhere" from a prior publication rather than claiming to create or significantly extend software themselves (S2).

The paper is a methodological/simulation study comparing versions of the Lagrange multiplier test. For data: it generates extensive synthetic Monte Carlo simulation data under various misspecification scenarios (clearly "generated" data per the criteria's explicit example of synthetic data), and it also applies the tests to an existing real dataset (Miller et al., 1984) which is "used" rather than generated. Since the paper both generates and uses data, the general rule assigns it to the generated category (D1). For software: the authors rely on existing R tools (the base "optim" function, and the "NumDeriv" and "ltm" R packages) to implement estimation and numerical derivatives; there is no claim of having created or significantly extended a standalone research software tool/package, nor any code-sharing/software contribution statement. This constitutes use of existing research software rather than generation of new software (S2).

The paper's core contribution is the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, an online software tool whose scoring algorithm, logic, and components were designed and built as part of this research (S1 - software generated), even though implementation was contracted to a third party. The research also generated new data: expert judgement and evidence-assessment scores for hundreds of actions and species groups across biomes, produced via structured Delphi-style elicitation workshops and panels (reported in Table 2 and Supplementary Table S12). This qualifies as D1 (data generated), since it is newly created research data rather than merely reused existing data (the Conservation Evidence database and the example farm's data are used as inputs, but the elicited scoring dataset underlying the metric is a novel research output).

The paper reports original experimental data (PXRD, DSC, FTIR, dissolution measurements on newly prepared ibuprofen-polymer solid dispersions), which constitutes generated research data (D1). The only software mentioned (EVA, TA Universal Analysis, OMNIC) are vendor instrument/data-processing utilities used merely to analyze spectra/thermograms, not research software created, extended, or claimed as a contribution, so this falls under S3 (No Research Software).

This is a historical/art-history essay analyzing archival letters, exhibition catalogues, and literature (RIBA archives, National Art Library records) to construct a narrative about Oliver Hill's exhibition design in 1933. It does not involve any research software (no code, tools, or computational methods created or used). The sources consulted are archival documents and literature/correspondence, which the criteria explicitly classify as 'Not Research Data' (literature, papers, protocols), rather than research data collected/generated/derived through a research method. No dataset is compiled, generated, or statistically analyzed. Hence neither software nor data criteria are met.

This is a PRISMA-ScR scoping review that systematically searches and synthesizes findings from seven previously published clinical studies on fluoride mouthwashes' effects on orthodontic appliances. No research software was created or used as a contribution—Excel and EndNote are mentioned only as general-purpose utility tools for recording search results and removing duplicates, which falls under "not research software" (generic data processing/reference management tools). The paper's inputs are literature/published papers, which the criteria explicitly classify as "Not Research Data." No new research data (e.g., experiments, measurements, surveys) were generated or used; the authors extracted and narratively summarized findings from existing publications, which does not count as research data under the given definitions.

The paper reports a novel crystal structure determined by X-ray diffraction, generating new research data (atomic coordinates, bond geometry, CCDC deposition 1537099) — this is D1. For software, the authors used existing established crystallographic programs (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND) without claiming to have created or extended any software themselves, so this is S2.

The paper reports an evaluation study that generated new research data: interview transcripts and focus group recordings from 22 teachers, plus a supplementary survey of lead schools. This qualifies as research data generated (D1). The only software mentioned is NVivo, used generically for coding/qualitative analysis; it is a widely-used generic data analysis tool not created or extended by the researchers and not claimed as a research contribution, so it falls under S3 (No Research Software).

This is a literature review summarizing published experimental and computational studies on protein-ionic liquid interactions (keratins, collagens, silks, enzymes, etc.), compiling solubility data, conditions, and findings from cited works into tables. The authors do not create or use any research software themselves (COSMO-RS, MD simulations etc. are performed by the cited studies, not the review authors) — this is S3. They do draw on and synthesize existing published research data/findings (solubility values, experimental results) from the literature to inform their discussion, which constitutes D2 (data used, including findings/statistics derived from existing sources), but they do not generate any new data themselves.

This is a qualitative, interpretive case study (no research software created or used—just standard content analysis of qualitative material, not a software contribution). The authors generated original research data through 25 personal interviews, non-participant observation, and archival/document research conducted over a longitudinal fieldwork period (2007–2014), which constitutes clear evidence of research data generation (D1), while no research software is mentioned anywhere (S3).

The paper reports original experimental measurements (PL spectra, ODMR spectra, g2(τ) intensity-correlation traces, confocal images) generated specifically for this study, clearly constituting generated research data (D1). The paper also states "The codes used for the analysis included in the current study are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request" and describes custom kinetic/spin-Hamiltonian simulation models (bi-/tri-exponential fitting, S=1 and S=3/2 ODMR spectrum simulations) developed specifically to analyze and model their data, rather than relying on named pre-existing research software packages. This custom-built analysis/simulation code constitutes generated research software (S1), since there is no indication it is merely a generic plotting/utility tool and no existing software is cited as having been used.
